lines.en: Dawn. Day seven. There's a rope around your neck, and the whole village came to watch.
In your tied hands, you're holding the only thing in this century that can save you. A phone. One percent battery.
Come on... come on. Please, just turn on.
Seven days ago, you didn't know this village existed. Seven days ago, you were almost eight hundred years away from it.
It started with a summer job. The night shift at a university archive, scanning old books nobody has opened in centuries.
Tonight's book is a chronicle, written by monks in a small English village called Netherwick, in the year twelve fifty-three.
Page after page of harvests, storms and dead cows. And then, in the margin... a drawing.
A man in a hoodie, holding a small glowing rectangle. With your face.
Okay. What... is this?
Under the drawing, someone has pencilled a translation.
In this year, a stranger fell from the sky into our village. He spoke in strange tongues and carried a stone of light. On the seventh day, he was hanged.
You take a picture of the page. For your friends. Nobody's going to believe this.
Then you touch the drawing... and the ink is still wet.
The first thing you feel is cold mud. The second is a pig, very interested in your face.
No. No, no, no, no...
No road. No power lines. No sound of cars. Just fields, smoke, and a church bell somewhere far away.
Your phone: no signal, twenty-three percent. You switch it off. Something tells you you're going to need every single percent.
The village looks like a museum someone forgot to clean. Mud up to your ankles. Everything smells of smoke, animals and people.
Hwat art thou? Whennes comest thou?
That's English. Technically. You understand maybe one word in five. For the rest of this story... we'll translate.
Look at his shoes. Look at his clothes. He's not from here.
It's getting dark. Without thinking, you switch on your phone's flashlight.
That... was a mistake.
Witchcraft! He holds a star in his hand!
Pitchforks. A lot of pitchforks. And then a young monk pushes through the crowd.
Stop! If he is a devil, the Church will judge him. If he is a fool, God already has.
His name is Brother Aldric. He's the only person here who looks at you with more curiosity than fear.
He takes you to the priory. Rows of desks, ink pots, candles. This is where the monks write their books.
And there, on his desk, you see it. The same leather cover. The same book. Almost eight hundred years younger.
Our chronicle. I write down everything that happens in Netherwick. Every harvest, every storm.
You find the page with the drawing. It's empty. He hasn't written it yet. Which means it hasn't happened yet.
Six more days. I have six days to make sure this page says something else.
That's the deal. Change the end of the page, or the page ends you.
Day two starts with breakfast. A grey stew of beans and oats called pottage. Dark bread, hard as a brick. And ale.
Ale? For breakfast? Can I just get some water?
Water? From the river? Below the tannery? Water's for cows, love. Drink your ale.
In the Middle Ages, almost everyone drank weak ale, even children. Brewed was safer than a river full of everything the village throws into it.
You drink from the river anyway. By noon, you learn exactly why nobody else does.
You spend the rest of day two between a straw bed full of fleas, and a wooden hole in the ground.
Day three. You need food and a roof, so Maud gives you a job.
Can you plough? Shoe a horse? Mend a roof? Brew?
I can... make a website?
God help us. Carry the barrels.
Everything you know is useless here. You know how a phone works. Roughly. But you couldn't make a single nail.
That evening, the alehouse is packed. Hamo the reeve, the man who runs the lord's land, is playing dice with a travelling merchant. And losing. Badly.
You decide to film a little medieval vlog. For when you get home. Proof nobody will ever believe.
Take the cup. The lord's silver cup. And not one word to anyone.
You don't think much about it. You're tired, and your shoulders hurt from the barrels.
Day four. The bell rings at the wrong time. The whole village gathers at the manor.
The lord's silver cup is gone! Stolen from the manor in the night!
And who came to this village four days ago? Who carries the devil's stone?
Everyone turns to look at you.
In medieval England, stealing anything worth more than twelve pence could send you to the gallows. A silver cup is worth a lot more than twelve pence.
They search you. They find the phone. The reeve holds it up like proof.
The devil's stone! Give it to the priests. Let them burn it.
And you, they throw into the cellar under the manor.
Day five. The manor court. The lord is away, so his steward judges. The jury is twelve men from the village.
This lord has an old right called infangthief: the right to hang a thief caught on his own land. No king's judge needed.
I didn't take anything! I was carrying barrels all night! Ask Maud!
He was with me till the last candle. The boy can't even light a fire!
She'd say anything for a strong back that works for free.
Nobody here knows you. No family, no lord, no one to speak for you. To them, a stranger is the easiest answer.
Guilty. You'll hang at dawn on the seventh day. Exactly like the chronicle said.
Day six. Night. Footsteps outside the bars. Brother Aldric. And under his robe... your phone.
They gave it to me to burn. I couldn't. I need to know what you are.
You switch it on. Eighteen percent. You show him the photo from the archive.
His own handwriting. His own drawing. In a book that looks almost eight hundred years old.
That's... my hand. My page. But I haven't written it yet.
You will. Unless we change it. I didn't steal the cup, Aldric. Hamo lost it at dice. And I can prove it.
You show him the video. He watches it three times.
If they see this, they'll call it witchcraft. But if they hear it... they'll know Hamo's voice.
There's a plan. It's a terrible plan. And you have four percent.
Dawn. Day seven. The rope. The crowd. Right where we started. And the cold has eaten the battery down to one percent.
Aldric asks the steward for one thing: let the condemned man hold the devil's stone, so the whole village can watch the evil die with him. The steward likes a good show. He agrees.
You press play. And turn the volume all the way up.
Take the cup. The lord's silver cup. And not one word to anyone.
The crowd goes silent. Everybody knows that voice.
Witchcraft! The stone speaks with the devil's tongue!
The devil doesn't lose at dice, Hamo. You do. Every Saturday.
The jury that condemned you turns around. The steward signals to his men. And this time, it's the reeve they drag away.
Your phone goes dark. Zero percent. It saved your life with its very last breath.
That night, in the priory, Aldric opens the chronicle at the empty page.
So. How does it end? Tell me, and I'll write it.
Write that the stranger went home.
Then leave me the stone. Otherwise no one will ever believe me.
Fair enough. Thank you, Aldric. For believing me.
He draws you in the margin. The hoodie, the shoes, the little dark stone. You touch the drawing. The ink is still wet.
Three in the morning. The archive. Your desk. Your hands are empty.
You open the chronicle. The drawing is still there. But the last line has changed.
On the seventh day, the stranger went home. He left us his stone of light, which never spoke again.
And in the archive's catalogue, under Netherwick Priory, there's one more item. Found in the ruins in nineteen seventy-two. A small black slab of glass. Purpose unknown.
Almost eight hundred years ago, one person in that whole village believed you. Sometimes, that's all it takes.
If you woke up in the Middle Ages tomorrow, what's the one thing you'd want in your pocket? Tell me in the comments.
